# Applied Replication for Data Skills {#europeanisation-and-the-economy .unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.home-lead}
Applied Replication for Data Skills (AR4DS) is a hands-on course that introduces social data science tools and statistical methods through the reanalysis of a published finding. The focal published finding comes from an article reanalysed as part of [SCORE (Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence)](https://www.cos.io/score), a large-scale, multi-method research initiative designed to improve the assessment of scientific credibility in the social and behavioural sciences. Operationalising scientific credibility as the 'repeatability' of research findings, SCORE subjected an initial selection of 600 academic publications to three tests: whether published results can be *reproduced* with the original data and code; to what extent a central finding is *robust* to alternative analytical choices; and whether the finding can be *replicated* using new data.

On this site, the published finding is a claim of an analysis of Eurobarometer surveys conducted between 2004 and 2013, which asked whether the economic crisis had changed the meanings that citizens attach to the European Union [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic].
:::

::: {.home-cta}
[Formats](#formats) [Read the case background](background.qmd)
:::

## The course {#the-course .unnumbered}

::: {.home-intro}
The main aim of the course is to introduce technical skills for modern empirical data analysis: finding the data and code of a study in an online repository, working with code so that another person (or your future self) can reproduce your steps, fixing your analytical choices in a preregistration before you run the analysis, and writing a live report that combines code and text.
:::

The claim at the centre of the exercise comes from the work of SCORE, a programme that put claims from published social and behavioural research through reproduction, robustness checks and replication. The exercise follows the design of the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] on a smaller scale, with many analysts testing the same claim, each stating their analytical choices, and results reported in a form that allows them to be compared. The SCORE page of the AR4DS site describes [the programme and its robustness study](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/score.html), including how the results of the analysts were placed on [one scale](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/score.html#sec-scale) and compared.

::::

:::: {.home-rs .home-reveal}

::: {.home-r}
### Reproduction {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Participants choose one of the three reanalyses fitted on aggregate data and repeat it step by step, recovering the recorded test statistic to the third decimal and establishing why the analysts arrived at such different estimates.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### Robustness {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Participants then work through the analytical decisions that lie between the data and a result, trying alternative specifications one change at a time, locating each result on a specification curve of `r e_spec` defensible analyses and – in the full-day and self-taught formats – declaring one specification in a short preregistration before it is run.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### Replication {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The course then sets the claim against its replication in the SCORE replicability study, on fourteen later Eurobarometer waves, which was judged not successful, and considers what a failed replication can and cannot establish about the original result.
:::

## The case study {#the-case .unnumbered}

::: {.home-intro}
The case study is built around an article published in the *European Sociological Review* in 2016, which drew on Eurobarometer surveys conducted between 2004 and 2013 to examine whether the economic crisis had changed the meanings that citizens attach to the European Union, or what its author calls 'EU framing'. One sentence of its abstract, in the form given to the analysts of the robustness study, became the claim tested in the course:
:::

> "... poor economic performances ... decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 619]

::: {.home-cta}
[Read the case background](background.qmd)
:::

::::

:::: {.home-rs .home-reveal}

::: {.home-r}
### Methods {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The aggregation of repeated cross-sections into a panel, fixed and random effects and the within–between model, inference with few clusters, and a multiverse of `r e_spec` specifications.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### Data {.unnumbered .unlisted}

A panel of `r e_cells` country-years built from the Eurobarometer surveys and shipped with the workspace. The respondent files behind it come from the GESIS archive, under a free account and terms that do not allow them to be passed on. Extending the analysis to later waves, as the SCORE replicability study did with fourteen waves fielded between 2013 and 2019, needs the respondent files of those waves from GESIS, under the same terms, and the unemployment and growth series of the World Bank for the same years.
:::

## Formats {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The facilitator of a course chooses its format, and the link that you receive for a course leads to it, as does the card of each format below.
:::

:::: {.home-grid}

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### [Part-day](tracks/short/index.qmd) {#short .unnumbered .unlisted}

[Two halves, with R inside the slides]{.home-meta}

Three hours on the claim and its five reanalyses, with nothing to install and nothing preregistered: the estimand statement, the reproduction of one recorded result, the specification menu with your own tries on the class chart, the curve of 864 and how to read it, and the replication with new data.
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### [Full-day](tracks/day/index.qmd) {#day .unnumbered .unlisted}

[Four parts, in the workspace]{.home-meta}

The claim and the credibility of social science, with the record of the paper in SCORE, the estimand and the causal graph, the reproduction of one of the reanalyses that worked on country-years, chosen by each participant, and the robustness exercise: the specification menu, the class chart and its submissions, the curve of the claim, and one analysis declared before it runs.
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### [Self-taught](tracks/independent/index.qmd) {#independent .unnumbered .unlisted}

[At your own pace, in R]{.home-meta}

The case study for a reader who works alone, in R on your own machine, with the modules of the [companion](companion/index.qmd) between the tasks of the exercise and a project of your own at the end.
:::

## Companion {#the-companion .unnumbered}

::: {.home-intro}
The companion curriculum holds the modules that teach the skills around the exercise, in three groups: the tools with which an analysis is written, the data and the public records that allow others to find an analysis and run it again, and the statistical methods of the case study. Every module is written on the data of the case study, and none is required for the part-day and full-day formats, whose pages point to some modules as preparation before a session, to others as the slower companion of one of its parts, and to the rest as reading for afterwards. The self-taught format works through the modules in its stages, between the tasks of the exercise.
:::

::: {.home-cta}
[Open the companion](companion/index.qmd)
:::

## Resources {#the-resources .unnumbered}

::: {.home-intro}
The Resources page gathers what a participant may want to return to: a glossary of the terms that the course keeps apart, the public records of the case study and of its reanalyses, the core readings on SCORE, estimands, the multiverse and preregistration, the documentation of the tools, and the full list of the works cited on the site. The glossary and the records serve as preparation before a session, and the readings and the documentation as a way into the methods afterwards.
:::

A social scientist interested in the political sociology of migration, mobility, ethnicity and nationalism.

I approach social research as a comparative, interdisciplinary and multimethodological endeavour. My work has combined ethnographic observation, document analysis, survey methods and statistical modelling.

I'm enthusiastic about transparency and reproducibility in the social sciences, and my [pedagogical approach](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/mediav8/library/file-downloads/research-services/open-research/moreh.pdf) seeks to develop skills that facilitate open and credible research practices.

## AI disclosure {.unnumbered}

The course grew out of a short session written for an open research conference at Newcastle University, which was built on my own reanalysis of one claim in the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. Its extension into the present course, with several case studies from SCORE and formats of different lengths, was carried out with the help of Claude models developed by Anthropic, used through Claude Code. The models were used to improve the websites and to design the formats, to check the R code and to find errors and inconsistencies across the materials, and to draft sections of the text of the pages, the slides and the workspaces. Everything that the models produced is being checked by me for its accuracy and its language.

AI assistants can also help participants during the course, with a piece of code that fails or as a partner in generating and testing ideas, used in a way that supports the work of the participant rather than replacing it, which means keeping the judgement of the analysis one's own and saying where the help came from. The module on [AI assistants](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/ai.html) sets out how to use one in the IDE, and its section on [licensed data](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/ai.html#sec-licensed) explains why the files of some case studies, such as the Eurobarometer surveys distributed by GESIS, may not be processed with an AI system at all.
